title: Chitta: The Riverbed Where Patterns Live
reflection: When an old reaction floods in bigger than the moment deserves, name it: this is an old channel, not today’s water. Then repeat one tiny luminous practice daily, however briefly.

questions.q: James disproves a verdict at 4 p.m., yet it is back at 9 a.m., fully formed. What does Swamiji say this is a clue to?
o: The pattern lives deeper than surface knowing: in chitta, the worker that stores and re-runs.
The pattern has not been properly disproved, so James needs a stronger argument against the verdict.
The pattern is a fault of memory, so James needs to practise forgetting the verdict at the end of a day.
The pattern is caused by the students, so it will stop when the students change what they do in class.
questions.e: Swamiji says that is not a failure on their part. Kai argues perfectly that one bad seminar does not make him worthless and it changes nothing: the feeling does not care what he knows. Why knowing better rarely changes the pattern is the puzzle the lesson answers.
questions.c: The pattern lives deeper than knowing

questions.q: In the image of the riverbed, what are the water, the bed, and the saṁskāras?
o: Water is present experience, the bed is chitta, the memory of past water, channels are saṁskāras.
The water is chitta, the bed is present experience, and the channels are the thoughts that cross the surface.
The water is the Self, the bed is the body, and the channels are the senses that carry the water along.
The water is memory, the bed is the future, and the channels are the choices that a person makes in time.
questions.e: Present experience runs along channels cut by past experience. A saṁskāra is more than a memory of what happened: it is a stored tendency that shapes what happens next.

questions.q: A child is scolded for every small mistake. Forty years later, as an adult, she feels dread over a tiny error nobody noticed. What does Swamiji say this shows?
o: A groove was cut, shame around imperfection: the events are long gone but the groove is still live.
A memory was kept, so that she can now recall each scolding in detail and is troubled by those events.
A habit was learned on purpose, so she can unlearn the dread whenever she decides that she will.
A fault was found in her character, so she must correct it by being firmer with herself in future.
questions.e: Sarah says this is almost exactly her own story and the thing she most fears repeating with her children. It cuts both ways: the same mechanism stores skill, as in a musician at the piano, and calm, as in a meditator’s years of quiet. The question is never whether it grooves but what gets grooved.
questions.c: The scoldings end; the groove stays live

questions.q: Kai can prove a thought is wrong, but it keeps winning. How does Swamiji explain the gap?
o: Knowing is a surface ripple and the saṁskāra is carved beneath: a ripple cannot re-carve a bed.
Knowing is weaker than feeling, so a person must learn to feel less strongly in order to be changed.
Knowing is correct but the argument is not, so Kai needs a better argument that fits his own case.
Knowing is of no value, so a person should drop reasoning and rely on practice and habit alone.
questions.e: The argument wins on points and loses in fact. James puts it: insight is real, it is just operating at the wrong depth. Swamiji says insight is necessary but works one layer up from where the pattern lives.
questions.c: A ripple cannot re-carve a riverbed

questions.q: “Left alone, the default direction of a groove is reinforcement: acting on it deepens it, so the patterns you run most become the ones you run most easily.”
questions.e: An experience leaves an impression; later something stirs it; it rises as a feeling you act on; the acting deepens the groove. Sarah sees that each leap to I’ve failed him deepens the channel. The same law is the way out: what you do not feed slowly silts up, and what you deliberately practise carves a new channel alongside.

questions.q: Kai says he is not broken for being unable to think his way out. What does Swamiji add about the therapies that help with stuck patterns?
o: They stop arguing and work on the stored impression, through body, repetition and safe re-experiencing.
They argue with the pattern more cleverly, so that the best thinking wins the exchange in the end.
They remove the stored impression altogether, so that the memory is deleted along with the pain.
They avoid the pattern altogether, so that nothing is done about the stored impression at the root.
questions.e: They rework the riverbed instead of shouting at the water. Swamiji says that sentence, you are not broken, is worth the whole lesson: Kai carries grooves cut under real conditions, doing exactly what grooves do.
questions.c: Rework the riverbed, not the water

questions.q: What does Pribram’s hologram picture say about memory, as the lesson uses it?
o: Memory is spread through the brain, and as in a hologram the whole is in every fragment, dimmer.
Memory is filed in one place, and as in a drawer a missing page leaves a permanent gap in the whole.
Memory is a recording, and as on a tape each moment is kept exactly as it first happened and for good.
Memory is a copy of the world, and as in a mirror it can show only what is in front of it at the time.
questions.e: That is why one deep impression can tint everything: a single trauma can reorganise a person’s whole way of being, not by magic but because in a holographic field the part carries the whole. Swamiji links it to the seed and tree of the Pratyabhijñā Hṛdayam and to the Gītā: three roads pointing at one strange truth.

questions.q: Sarah asks whether one luminous impression can work the other way. What does Swamiji answer?
o: Fully yes: one genuine moment of peace or clarity does not stay in its corner but seeds the field.
No: only dark impressions spread, and a luminous one stays small and is lost among the darker ones.
Yes, but only after the dark impressions have all been removed from the field by a long practice.
Yes, but only when the luminous impression is a very large one, such as a great vision or a rare insight.
questions.e: This is why the traditions are so particular about what you expose yourself to, practise and repeat: not moralising, engineering. Every impression becomes part of the living pattern of the whole field.
questions.c: One luminous saṁskāra seeds the whole

questions.q: “Chitta-śuddhi, the purifying of the mind-field, means erasing your memory so that wounds are deleted.”
questions.e: Erasing memory would wipe out skills and love along with wounds. It is re-landscaping the riverbed: letting reactive, fear-cut channels silt up while carving new, clearer ones, through a repeated word or breath, meditation, good company, service and time with what is true and beautiful.

questions.q: When Kai’s “I am worthless” floods in after a stumble, what does the practical experiment ask of him?
o: Name it, not argue: “old groove, not today’s water,” then carve: thirty seconds of breath daily.
Argue it down, so that the thought has no ground left, and then give his attention to something else.
Wait until it passes, so that no new groove is cut, and then do nothing more about it until next time.
Push it away, so that it cannot deepen, and think of something cheerful until it has gone from sight.
questions.e: Kai is not going to win the argument; he is going to re-landscape, one repetition at a time. Sarah is to name her shame-groove, my riverbed and not a fact about my son, and give each child one warm unhurried moment a day. James is to begin one lesson with thirty seconds of calm.
questions.c: Name the groove, carve a new one
